reference.source: Murray and Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: Middle lobe syndrome denotes recurrent or chronic collapse, consolidation or bronchiectasis of the right middle lobe, and by extension the lingula.

Anatomical predisposition is central: the right middle lobe bronchus is long and narrow, arises at an acute angle, and is surrounded by a collar of lymph nodes, with relatively poor collateral ventilation to the lobe.
It is classified into obstructive forms (endobronchial tumour, broncholith, extrinsic nodal compression, foreign body) and non-obstructive forms (recurrent infection, asthma, impaired clearance).
In adults, a persistently collapsed middle lobe must prompt exclusion of an endobronchial neoplasm before it is assumed to be benign.
In children and non-smokers, asthma, recurrent infection and impaired mucociliary clearance are common non-obstructive causes.
Presentation includes chronic cough, recurrent focal pneumonia, wheeze and haemoptysis, or it may be an incidental radiographic finding.
The lateral chest radiograph shows a characteristic thin, wedge-shaped opacity overlying the cardiac shadow; CT delineates bronchiectasis, volume loss and any obstructing lesion.

Bronchoscopy is central to excluding an obstructing lesion and obtaining microbiological and cytological samples; non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection (the 'Lady Windermere' pattern) is an important association.
reference.pathophysiology: The right middle lobe is anatomically vulnerable: its bronchus is comparatively long and slender, branches at an acute angle from the bronchus intermedius, and is encircled by hilar and interlobar lymph nodes, while collateral ventilation from adjacent lobes is limited because the lobe is largely surrounded by fissures. Any process that narrows the bronchus — an endobronchial tumour, broncholith, aspirated foreign body, or extrinsic compression by enlarged nodes — readily produces atelectasis with impaired clearance and post-obstructive infection. In non-obstructive disease, recurrent infection, asthma or ciliary and clearance defects lead to mucus retention and repeated inflammation; because collateral ventilation cannot easily re-expand the lobe, atelectasis persists and a cycle of infection, inflammation and bronchial wall damage ensues, culminating in bronchiectasis and chronic volume loss. Non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection may both result from and perpetuate this process, classically in the middle lobe and lingula.
additionalDifferentials: broncholithiasis obstructing the middle lobe bronchus
extrinsic nodal compression from sarcoidosis, tuberculosis or malignancy
recurrent aspiration or asthma-related mucus plugging
additionalInvestigations: chest CT with attention to the middle lobe bronchus, nodes and bronchiectasis
flexible bronchoscopy to exclude obstruction and obtain samples
sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage for bacteria, mycobacteria and fungi
cytology or biopsy of any endobronchial lesion
pulmonary function testing and assessment for asthma
evaluation for impaired mucociliary clearance or immunodeficiency in recurrent disease
tuberculin or interferon-gamma release testing where granulomatous disease is suspected
redFlags: haemoptysis or an endobronchial lesion suggesting malignancy
persistent lobar collapse in an adult smoker
systemic features such as weight loss or night sweats
recurrent pneumonia confined to the same lobe despite treatment
progressive bronchiectasis with worsening sputum burden
reference.prognosis: Non-obstructive disease often improves with treatment of infection, airway inflammation and clearance, whereas established bronchiectasis or an obstructing lesion may require targeted therapy or surgical resection; outcome is generally good once malignancy is excluded and the underlying cause addressed.
pitfalls: Assuming benign disease and omitting bronchoscopy in an adult with a persistently collapsed middle lobe.
Overlooking non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection as both cause and consequence of the syndrome.
Missing a small obstructing broncholith or foreign body on low-resolution imaging.
Attributing recurrent focal pneumonia to simple community infection without pursuing the anatomical explanation.
Proceeding to resection without adequately characterising and treating a reversible infective or inflammatory cause.
references: Murray and Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine, current edition
Fishman's Pulmonary Diseases and Disorders, current edition
Contemporary reviews of right middle lobe syndrome and non-tuberculous mycobacterial lung disease
management: Exclude and relieve endobronchial obstruction bronchoscopically, removing a foreign body or broncholith and treating any endobronchial tumour
Treat non-obstructive causes by optimising asthma control with inhaled corticosteroids and treating infection with appropriate antibiotics
Promote airway clearance with chest physiotherapy and secretion-clearance techniques, especially where bronchiectasis is present
Treat recurrent or post-obstructive infection with targeted antibiotic therapy guided by sputum and lavage cultures
Consider surgical resection (middle lobectomy) for refractory disease, established localised bronchiectasis or a resectable obstructing lesion
Investigate and manage underlying impaired mucociliary clearance or immunodeficiency in recurrent disease
Follow up with imaging to confirm resolution and ensure malignancy has been excluded
